Since some one started a thread about reloading I thought I would throw in my 7 cents worth. (2 cents adjusted for inflation). First of all guys the lack of ammunition and reloading powder is a function of the market. There just aren't that many plants making smokeless powder anymore. In fact there are only three smokeless powder plants on the North American continent. General Dynamics owns the ST. Marks Florida plant and the Canadian plant that used to make the IMR (stick) powders. BAE systems out of Europe runs the Radford Arsenal plant (contractor to the US Government) Then three smokeless powder plants in Europe. One owned by Thales, one Owned by Reinmetal, and owned by SNPE group. (There are some plants in the former Eastern block mostly in Russia. There is also one in Serbia.

Since the end of the cold war and the removal of private owned weapons in the rest of the world the demand for smokeless powder has evaporated. Also the heavy environmental and siting regulations have made it impossable open up new plants.

Now on to the powder its self. The base for smokeless powder was the discovery of Nitrocellulose in 1847. Nitrocellulose is nothing more than common cotton treated by 7 parts Concentrated Sulfuric acid and 3 parts of Nitric acid. The cotton is soaked in the mixture for about 20 minutes than washed in water and a weak base to remove the acid. when the cotton is dried it decomposes very rapidly when exposed to heat. (it really doesn't burn as it doesn't take up oxygen in the combustion process.) In fact nitrocellulose burns so fast that you can hold it in your hand while it decomposes and it won't burn you.

The next step in making smokeless powder is to turn the nitrocellulose into a gelatin. (By the way old photographic film base was nitrocellulose gelatin dried into thin sheets.) Most plants use nitroglycerin to perform the gelatinization process. Once the nitrocellulose is a gelatin it is squirted through various dies into a alcohol bath to harden the finished product. The dies can be made to squirt out solid stick, hollowed out sticks, spherical, or flake products.

Once the smokeless powder is dried it is coated with graphite (a from of pure carbon) to keep it from clumping and to make it easier to meter in the filling of cartridges and shells.

Now down to the nitty gritty. The decomposing process is started by the application of heat and pressure. The speed of decomposing is a function of the size of the powder. The greater the surface area the faster the decomposition. So a large stick will have a large surface area that gets smaller as the stick decomposes. If you make a hollow center in the stick the decomposition from the inside about equals out the decomposition of the outside. If you make multiple holes in the stick the decomposition accelerates over time. Flake powder burns fastest of all because it is almost all surface area. Spherical powder is also fast decomposing though not a fast as flake.

Now what does all this stuff mean. Well for those who want to do reloading manuals have a couple pages dedicated to the decomposing speed of various powders (here is where the powder companies screw up they generally list powders from all manufactures). Most start with the slowest powders going to the fastest. Now if you are feeling adventurous you can develop your own loads for almost any powder. You start with an known powder (slowest burning) from a commercial loading manual. (Hint here each powder company only lists the powder they sell and not any one eases) Then you go to the fastest power in the loading manual. When you have the loading data of the two powders you go back to the list of powders in the slowest to fastest powders and select a powder that lies between the two Use the loading data for the least pressure from the loading data manual. load up a round or two. Fire them off and inspect the brass for over pressure. If you see that the primer is flattened or the head stamp on the base has been upset or you have a hole blown through the primer you are in deep fecal material, and DON'T DO THAT ANYMORE!!!!! If on the other hand the primer still has the rounded edges and the case extracts very easily then your pressure is good and you can increase the powder loader in 1/10 grain increments. Don't worry about velocity. It is pressure that you are concerned with.

Now you know all you never wanted to know about smokeless powder..JD
